Vendor Monitoring Long read
Third-Party Data Breach Notification Timelines and Regulatory Obligations
Vendors' notification delays now become their customers' compliance deadlines.
Theo Barajas
October 1, 2026 · 11 min read
Vendor Monitoring · October 1, 2026 · 11 min read · 2,511 words
A telecommunications company called Bluepeak discovered a cybersecurity incident in December 2025. Clarity Telecom, LLC d/b/a Bluepeak (No. 1: 26 -cv-02251, filed May 22, 2026), where the company discovered the breach in December 2025 but did not begin notifying customers until May 2026. The case marks a shift in how breach litigation works: plaintiffs and regulators are no longer only asking why a breach happened. They are asking why notification took so long, and that question sits squarely on top of a legal mechanism that most organizations have not built their vendor programs to survive.
California's SB 446, in effect since January 1, 2026, makes the mechanism explicit. When the entity that suffers a breach does not own the data involved, it must notify the data owner or licensee immediately after discovering the breach. The data owner then has 30 days from that notification to inform the affected individuals. The data owner's clock does not start at the moment of the breach. It starts at the moment the vendor gets around to saying something, and nothing in the statute pauses that 30-day window while the data owner waits on a slow or reluctant supplier.
Regulatory notification obligations attach to whichever organization holds the relationship with the affected individual, regardless of which party in the supply chain actually caused the incident, so a vendor's internal delay becomes the customer's compliance exposure. A vendor's internal delay, whether from a slow forensic investigation, an unclear chain of internal approval, or simple reluctance to disclose bad news, gets transferred directly into the notifying organization's own compliance exposure. The vendor's problem becomes the customer's deadline. Every section that follows works through what that transfer looks like in practice, and why most organizations are not currently positioned to absorb it.
The patchwork of deadlines for a multistate organization
An organization operating across state lines manages dozens of breach notification deadlines at once. It is managing dozens of them, each running on its own clock, each triggered by its own definition of "discovery," and each carrying its own penalty structure for missing it. As of January 1, 2026, roughly two in five U.S. states have replaced vague standards with a specific numeric deadline. The rest still rely on language such as "without unreasonable delay," which sounds forgiving until a regulator or a plaintiff's attorney decides it was not fast enough.
California, Colorado, Florida, New York, and Washington require notice within 30 days. Alabama, Arizona, Indiana, Ohio, Oregon, and a number of other states allow 45 days . 30-day states now include California, Colorado, Florida, New York, and Washington; 45-day states include Alabama, Arizona, Indiana, Ohio, Oregon, and others; 60-day states include Connecticut, Delaware, and Louisiana. New York tightened its own window in 2025, and Oklahoma updated its breach statute for the first time since 2008, through SB 626, effective January 1, 2026, adding a requirement to notify the state Attorney General when 500 or more residents are affected.
Individual notice is only the first clock. Under California SB 446, businesses that notify more than 500 California residents must send a copy of that notice to the state Attorney General within 15 calendar days of notifying individuals, its own hard deadline. More broadly, over two-thirds of states require some form of report to the Attorney General or another state agency, but fewer than half of those states make the resulting data publicly accessible, so regulators end up holding breach information that the consumers those regulators are supposed to protect cannot easily find.
Federal and sector-specific rules stack on top of the state patchwork rather than replacing it. The SEC's cybersecurity disclosure rule requires public companies to file an 8-K for a material cybersecurity incident within four business days of determining materiality. GDPR requires notice to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of the controller becoming aware, the tightest clock in wide use anywhere. For organizations with EU exposure or financial-sector ties, NIS2 adds a 24-hour early warning and a 72-hour incident notification for essential and important entities, and regulators have already begun enforcing it: NIS2 issued its first administrative penalties for untimely reporting in the first quarter of 2026. DORA formalizes ICT risk governance and incident reporting for the financial sector and its technology suppliers; the first list of critical ICT third-party providers was published November 18, 2025, with operational supervision building through 2026. DORA's enforceability, effective since January 2025, has extraterritorial reach , placing U.S. fintech vendors with EU bank customers in scope.
None of this is confined to breach notification statutes anymore. States including Delaware, Iowa, Nebraska, New Hampshire, Minnesota, Tennessee, New Jersey, Maryland, Indiana, Kentucky, and Rhode Island have built general security requirements directly into comprehensive privacy laws, often with tougher standards for sensitive categories of data. A breach response plan built only around the notification statute can miss obligations that now live elsewhere in the code. Building one internal response standard around the most lenient deadline in this list, the old habit for organizations trying to simplify a messy landscape, is no longer defensible. It is a documented gap waiting for a regulator or a plaintiff to find it.
How the third-party notification cascade consumes the time those clocks allow
Every one of those deadlines assumes the notifying organization knows what happened. When a vendor causes the breach, that assumption breaks down, and the clock keeps running anyway.
Walk through the mechanics under SB 446. The data owner 's 30-day window does not begin until the breached vendor actually sends notification. If that vendor spends two weeks on internal escalation, scope confirmation, and legal review before notifying the data owner, the data owner inherits a 30-day clock with roughly half its runway already gone, and still has to investigate the incident from its own side, draft notice language, route it through legal and compliance review, and distribute it to affected individuals. The same structure appears under GDPR, where the 72-hour clock runs from the moment the controller becomes aware. If a data processor sits on that information even briefly before passing it along, the controller's clock has already been running before the controller knew there was a clock at all. DORA compresses the same problem into hours rather than days: a financial entity has four hours from classifying an incident as major to file its initial notification, and a vendor that takes even a short internal investigation window before alerting its financial institution customer can cause that institution to miss the obligation outright.
Investigation timelines make the compression worse. Determining the scope of a breach, the categories of data involved, and the geographic residence of affected individuals is not fast work, even with significant resources applied to it, and the earlier a regulatory clock starts relative to that investigation, the less accurate the eventual notice tends to be. Connecticut regulators have clarified that the state's 60 -day window starts from the date a company becomes aware of suspicious activity rather than the date it fully understands the impact, a standard that other states may adopt as they revise their own laws. Layer onto that the average time it takes to detect and contain a supply chain attack: 254 days. No numeric notification deadline in current use, from California's 30 days down to DORA's four hours, was built to accommodate an eight-month detection window. Most third-party breaches are already running late before anyone outside the compromised vendor even knows they occurred.
Healthcare shows what this looks like at scale. In the first half of 2026, business associates made up a relatively small share of reported breach sources but were linked to a disproportionate share of the largest breaches, a pattern consistent with supply chain risk management coverage remaining one of the weakest areas in healthcare security programs as measured against NIST CSF functions. HIPAA's structure builds the cascade into the law itself: the business associate notifies the covered entity, and the covered entity then notifies HHS and the affected individuals. Each hand-off in that chain eats into the covered entity's 60-day window, a window the covered entity does not control the start of.
The gap underneath all of this is contractual. Vendor agreements should specify timely cyber incident reporting obligations that match the regulatory clocks the customer actually faces, but most agreements in force today predate the current wave of numeric state deadlines and still rely on qualitative language borrowed from an earlier legal environment. A clause requiring notification "without unreasonable delay" offers no real alignment to a 72-hour GDPR obligation or a 30-day California obligation once investigation time and cascade hand-offs are factored into the math. That contractual gap is where the legal architecture of notification meets the operational reality of how vendor risk programs are actually run, and it is where the next failure point sits.
Most vendor risk programs are not built to support a notification chain under time pressure
The contractual gap does not exist because vendor risk teams are careless. It exists because most third-party risk programs were built to answer a different question than the one a compressed notification deadline actually asks. Traditional vendor risk management measures whether a vendor passed an assessment at a point in time. A notification cascade under DORA's four-hour clock or GDPR's 72-hour clock asks something else: whether the organization knows, right now, what that vendor can access, what its current security posture looks like, and whether its contract can support a rapid disclosure chain. Those are different questions, and most programs were never built to answer the second one.
The Vendor Risk Management Maturity Model describes a path from reactive, ad hoc vendor oversight toward fully integrated, proactive risk management. Most organizations sit well short of that endpoint: both risk maturity and compliance maturity scores came in well below the maximum in the 2025 GRC benchmarking survey conducted by McKinsey. Banking regulators appear to see this as a live problem rather than an abstract one. Shared Assessments introduced an "Interagency Guidance Gap Analysis" alongside the 2025 VRMMM to help organizations implement guidance from the FDIC, FRB, and OCC.
How vendor risk gets measured in the first place accounts for part of the gap. Annual or periodic reviews capture a vendor's posture at a single moment , but that posture does not hold still between review cycles. Security configurations change, staff turn over, financial pressure builds, geopolitical exposure shifts, and incidents at a vendor's own sub-vendors alter the real risk picture in ways a fixed schedule cannot catch. A vendor that passed a SOC 2 audit six months earlier may have gone through a significant configuration change, lost key security staff, or absorbed an upstream supply chain compromise in the interim, and none of that would appear in the record until the next scheduled review comes around.
Where compliance teams spend their time compounds the problem. Much of the daily work in vendor risk management goes into collecting evidence, chasing down stakeholder attestations, and reconciling spreadsheet-based risk registers, activity that tracks how much work the team has done rather than how much risk a given vendor actually carries. A program built around that kind of activity can produce a completed questionnaire on demand, but it often cannot answer, on the first day of an incident, which vendors hold which categories of data, what each vendor's contract actually requires for notification, or whether those contractual terms match the specific jurisdictional deadlines the organization has to meet.
Healthcare again offers a measurable version of the pattern. The 2025 Healthcare Cybersecurity Benchmarking Study found supply chain risk management coverage and asset management among the weakest areas measured against NIST CSF functions, in a sector where HIPAA's notification cascade is explicitly defined and enforcement is active. A completed questionnaire is not worthless. It establishes a documented baseline, and that documentation matters for audit purposes. A questionnaire completed months earlier cannot tell an organization, on the first day of a breach, whether that vendor's posture has changed since the assessment, what data the vendor currently holds, or whether the vendor's own incident response plan can support a 24-hour notification. Documentation of a security posture that no longer reflects current reality functions as a liability once an incident starts, not a control.
Non-human identities and agentic integrations have created a new, largely unmapped layer of third-party breach exposure
The vendor relationships most TPRM programs assess are the ones formalized through contracts and onboarding reviews. A large and growing share of actual third-party access now runs through channels that never go through that process at all: OAuth tokens, service accounts, API keys, and credentials issued to SaaS plugins and increasingly to autonomous AI agents. In cloud-native environments, these non-human identities now outnumber human identities by a wide margin, and that ratio has grown sharply in just the past year as cloud adoption, microservices architecture, and SaaS integration have all expanded together.
These credentials behave differently from a human login, and the difference matters for how long a compromise can go unnoticed. An OAuth token grants durable, delegated access without the session controls applied to a person signing in: typically no multi-factor prompt, often no conditional access policy, and frequently no session timeout. A compromised long-lived refresh token can remain valid and usable for an extended period unless someone explicitly revokes it, rotates it, or it expires from inactivity. GitGuardian's 2026 data found that a meaningful minority of organizations have at least one publicly exposed asset carrying a long-lived, still-valid vendor secret, sitting outside the visibility of the vendor questionnaire process entirely.
The Salesloft Drift compromise, disclosed in August 2025, shows how this plays out at scale. The threat actor known as UNC6395 breached the backend of the Salesloft Drift AI integration and extracted long-lived OAuth access and refresh tokens issued across hundreds of Salesforce customer integrations, ultimately affecting more than 700 organizations. None of the organizations caught up in that incident experienced a failure in their own systems. They experienced a failure in a third-party integration's credential handling, one that most of them likely never named as a distinct vendor risk in the first place, because a chat integration or an AI plugin rarely goes through the same review process as a payment processor or a cloud hosting provider.
That is the exposure a notification cascade now has to account for. A breach originating in a non-human credential, issued to an AI agent or a SaaS integration that a vendor risk team never formally reviewed, still triggers the same regulatory clocks covered earlier in this piece. SB 446 's cascade notification and GDPR's 72-hour window still apply even when the compromised access point was a service account rather than a contracted vendor relationship. The notification chain runs on whether personal data was exposed, regardless of whether the access point that exposed it appeared anywhere on a vendor risk register. Until organizations extend their third-party risk mapping to cover these non-human identities with the same rigor applied to contracted vendors, this layer of exposure will keep sitting outside the process built to catch it, and it will fail the same way the Salesloft Drift tokens did.

Eugene Pilyankevich
Understanding cloud security #
In this article, we observe security responsibility of cloud providers: where it ends, what are the gaps and grey areas, and what risks security teams should take into account when using "as a service" platforms.
So, you're planning your new business in an area where security matters, and you start thinking about choosing your cloud provider to build your application on. Typically, you start juggling with a combination of all the nice building blocks you need and financial aspects you're facing.
At this stage, you might be thrilled with choices between IaaS and PaaS, or operating planet-scale cloud database. Yet, builders usually don't spend much time on clearly articulating cloud security strategy when they are thinking about starting their next project.
However, if you're in a regulated industry (like finance or healthcare) or face stringent requirements from your business environment (like in legal, insurance, fintech), there are security choices you need to contemplate as well.
In general, the mind prefers an answer like "it's a cloud, best security professionals are taking care of it" . Which is quite right (since the provider's team really polished their set of controls for millions of customers and stood the test of time with them), but this barely gives you a full picture.
New cloud users try to get peace of mind thinking "I've put it in a cloud, and cloud is secure" -that could be called risk outsourcing if it was true, but it's not.
What actually happens is "I've put it in a cloud, now I have to make it secure, but on cloud provider's on-prem and within limitations defined by the other party" - which looks more like risk sharing .
Cloud provider's security team takes care of many things. It's all true. But:
there are some things they can't do for you.
there are things they won't do for you. Alas.
there are things you shouldn't trust them anyway.
cloud provider's liability in worst case is far from what could make you sleep well at night.
Here we'd like to share a few observations made after deploying our products and building large-scale solutions in various restrictive cloud environments and aiding customers in improving security in their cloud-based solutions.
Shared responsibility model gaps
Definite gaps in a shared responsibility model
Cloud credentials and access control
Cloud configuration
Data security in a shared responsibility model
Application logic and code
Grey areas in shared responsibility model
More clouds-more gaps
Wrapping up & next steps
Despite the fact that many cloud providers clearly outline their (very limited!) area of responsibility in their usage policies, many customers still rely entirely (and blindly) on the cloud provider's security efforts.
In general, the application owner is responsible for system's security for everything that goes above the hypervisor level. Also, they must set up and configure the available security tools of cloud providers, like access control, firewall, logging, backups, etc.
Azure cloud shared responsibility model. Source Azure docs .
Publicly available S3 buckets without any authentication cause huge data leaks. A fresh one counted 24.4GB of data . It became such a typical mistake, that OWASP WSTG now has a separate requirement WSTG-CONF-11 and test case to cover S3 configuration issue.
To put it simply , depending on the cloud provider and their services, responsibilities are expressed as following:
IaaS : responsibility ends at hypervisor. Customers are responsible for application security, data security, middleware security, and host configuration and security.
PaaS : customers are still responsible for their custom applications, data security, application security (sometimes), interfaces, credentials, and platform configuration.
SaaS : customers are responsible for their credentials, interfaces, access, and data.
Shared responsibility model explained. Source Cloud Security Alliance .
In all these cases, access controls, identity management, data security, and control configuration are the customer's responsibility.
However, are cloud providers really responsible for the things they say they do?
AWS Customer Agreement (see 4. Your Responsibilities) says that "you are responsible for all activities that occur under your account, regardless of whether the activities are authorized by you or undertaken by you, your employees or a third party" and AWS "are not responsible for unauthorized access to your account."
Also, you're responsible for your content, for compliance to laws and data regulations, for backups and security, and for keeping your credentials and keys in secret.
You need to analyze whether a cloud provider's responsibilities are enforced in a way that fits your risk appetite, because even if the cloud provider takes responsibility for security incidents, it's unlikely that they will compensate for financial or reputational losses for your company when breach happens.
Now that we see the big picture, let's try to focus on the gaps and grey areas.
Cloud credentials and access control #
Admin control . If you don't design your systems in a clever way, once attackers get admin control over your console, it's game over. What's worse-it's gameover for your whole project, not just one server. Cloud providers are responsible for letting admin credentials owner to do everything they want-unless you've explicitly configured not to do that.
Service credentials . The lifecycle of keys, tokens, database passwords. You should define how to share keys across your development team members, how to notice leaked keys and rotate them.
User credentials . If you store users' passwords for authentication-you become responsible for managing their secrets.
Cloud configuration #
Service setup . As CapitalOne case shows, in the end you're responsible for services you've misconfigured (or were not aware that you have to configure them).
The data owner, but not the infrastructure operator, is held responsible for a breach under a number of regulations (GDPR, PCI, CCPA, country-wide regulations).
All you get from a cloud provider are basic controls, like data at rest encryption, and your provider has access keys and cryptographic keys to encrypted data.
You can either BYOK into your providers' infrastructure, or you can build your own protection layers (client-side encryption, or transparent field level encryption using tools like Acra ).
Application logic and code #
Whatever you produce-you own its security risks. Application security, dependency checks, patching vulnerabilities, security of your CRUD API, logging, monitoring, analytics of user behaviour, etc.-that's your responsibility.
Transparent field level encryption for your cloud databases: Acra database encryption suite. Easy-to-deploy and easy-to-manage searchable encryption with zero lines of crypto code.
Check out Acra
Identity and directory infrastructure : whether your IAM, directory service or whatever else is hosted locally or in-cloud, it's LDAP or some weird new tech-you are responsible for managing it, making it a reflection of your security policy that drives access control decisions, and monitoring it.
Networking : although your provider is responsible for core networking, everything that happens above virtualization is your problem, to some extent. Thus, you're likely to need to manage security-related configuration of relevant assets.
OS : depending on the type of cloud architecture you're pursuing, you might end up managing OS images yourself. While your cloud vendor provides you with base images of modern server operating systems, your job is to ensure they're secure and well-configured in your use-case.
Responsibility for security IN the cloud vs Responsibility for security OF the cloud. Source Amazon AWS Shared responsibility model .
More clouds-more gaps #
But these are not all the concerns. There are specific cases where aside from deciding where the responsibility is-you've got to actually understand how this responsibility is implemented and enforced:
Multi-cloud and hybrid cloud concerns: #
When your solution operates on multiple public clouds, you need to carefully map the gaps that are different between various cloud providers and ensure that core controls are consistent (or cloud agnostic).
You might want to have a compatibility layer for identity management, application level key management, enforcing the same data protection policies (encryption, tokenization, masking) between your clouds.
Cloud-based CI/CD pipeline: #
If your CI/CD pipeline takes place in a cloud, it becomes one of the primary targets for advanced attacks-unless you monitor and secure it well. Check out stories like XcodeGhost (patched Xcode version that silently injected malware into apps), M.E.Doc , and other supply chain attacks .
Mapping controls in attestation: #
Make a pause to map security controls from your cloud provider into your coverage map. Surprisingly, it could lead you to many uncomfortable questions we've outlined above. Especially, if you have third-party assessments providing any kind of attestation to your infrastructure, and "security control coverage" is something you have to obsess about.
You inherit some of the controls from your cloud, at least formally, but when you look at how much you really control in that security control-you don't control much.
While you can impress your auditors with this clever checklist trickery, attackers enthusiastically benefit from lack of practical attention to appropriate security controls.

Wrapping up & next steps #
When defining your cloud strategy, security risks should be treated equal to all others-with meticulous analysis. Because you're not "putting it in a cloud that's secure by design".
When you host your apps in a cloud, you are solely responsible for data security, appsec, managing secrets and accesses, and configuring tools providers give you.
Yes, you may win a lot by putting your assets in-cloud, but only if you're actually doing it with your eyes wide open.
